title: Thermal comfort in naturally ventilated buildings: revisions to ASHRAE Standard 55
authors: de Dear, Richard and Brager, Gail
review_question: To summarize the findings of ASHRAE RP-884 research on thermal comfort in naturally ventilated buildings and to describe the process and implications of incorporating an adaptive comfort standard into ASHRAE Standard 55.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Raw field data from various projects globally that followed a standardized (or similar) protocol for collecting physical and subjective thermal comfort data, meeting strict requirements for measurement techniques, data type, and database structure. For regression analyses, only buildings with statistically significant (P = 0.05) neutral or preferred temperature derivations were included.

evidence_base_summary.search_databases: Not applicable; data compiled from existing field studies following specific protocols.
evidence_base_summary.date_range: Field studies from mid-1980s onwards, compiled for RP-884.

findings.consequent: Indoor comfort temperature (Tcomf) in HVAC buildings
findings.quote: The adaptive model fitted by weighted regression to observed comfort temperatures has an R2 = 53% (P = 0.0001).

findings.consequent: Indoor comfort temperature (Tcomf) in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: The adaptive model fitted by weighted regression to observed comfort temperatures has an R2 = 70% (P = 0.0001).

findings.consequent: Observed indoor comfort temperatures in HVAC buildings
findings.quote: In the HVAC buildings, PMV was remarkably successful at predicting comfort temperatures, demonstrating that behavioral adjustments...fully explained the relationship.

findings.consequent: Observed indoor comfort temperatures in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: in the NV buildings (Fig. 2b), the difference between these PMV-based predic- tions and the adaptive model (fitted to OBS) shows that such behavioral adjustments accounted for only half of the climatic dependence of comfort temperatures.

findings.consequent: Optimum comfort temperature (Tcomf) for naturally ventilated buildings (Adaptive Comfort Standard equation)
Acceptable comfort zone width for naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: a mean comfort zone band of 5 °C for 90% acceptability, and 7 °C for 80% acceptability, both centered on the optimum comfort temperature.

findings.consequent: Indoor thermal sensation regression model gradient (thermal sensitivity) in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: The sensitivity of indoor thermal sensations to changes in indoor temperature (y-axis) shows no relationship to outdoor climate (x-axis).

findings.consequent: Indoor operative temperatures and thermal sensations in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: below mean outdoor temperatures of 23 °C, the NV build- ings were primarily operating within the limits of the ACS, and mean thermal sensations were primarily within ±0.5.

findings.consequent: Indoor operative temperatures and thermal sensations in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: Above mean outdoor temperatures of 23 °C, interior temperatures frequently rose above the ACS limits, with mean indoor operative temperatures clustered around 30 °C, and simultaneous mean thermal sensations clustered around a mean vote of 1.0.

findings.antecedent: Application of Adaptive Comfort Standard (ACS) compared to ASHRAE Standard 55
findings.quote: The map shows the regions of the country where the difference in comfort temperatures using these two methods ranges from 0 to 5 °C. Energy savings would be proportional to the difference in these set-points.

synthesis_conclusions: The adaptive model provides a more accurate representation of thermal comfort in naturally ventilated buildings compared to the PMV model, accounting for psychological adaptation.
The new Adaptive Comfort Standard (ACS) allows for warmer indoor temperatures in naturally ventilated buildings, particularly in warmer climates, potentially leading to significant energy savings.
Personal control over the thermal environment (e.g., operable windows) is crucial for enabling adaptive responses and influencing thermal expectations.
The ACS is applicable under specific conditions for naturally conditioned spaces, where occupants have control and engage in sedentary activity.

There is a need for further research into the psychological dimensions of adaptation, the role of personal control, and the integration of thermal comfort with other indoor environmental quality factors.
evidence_gaps: How to best characterize outdoor climate for adaptive models (e.g., daily vs. monthly averages, recent history, forecasts).
Better ways to assess dissatisfaction or acceptability than indirect association with thermal sensation votes.
The assumption that inter-individual differences are the same in laboratory and field settings.
Impact of clothing patterns (fashion vs. adaptation, gender differences) on thermal comfort and adaptation.
The role of perceived vs. utilized control in thermal comfort and expectations.
Optimizing thermal comfort, indoor air quality, energy, and productivity simultaneously.
Understanding the impact of personal control on comfort, health, productivity, and energy use.
Moving beyond thermal neutrality to 'thermal delight' and stimulating thermal environments.
Research on mixed-mode buildings and task/ambient conditioning systems within the adaptive framework.

moderators.effect: HVAC buildings show less adaptation to outdoor temperature changes (flatter slope for comfort temperature vs. outdoor temperature) compared to naturally ventilated buildings (steeper slope). The PMV model is more successful in HVAC buildings.
moderators.subgroup_effects: HVAC buildings: R² = 53% for adaptive model; NV buildings: R² = 70% for adaptive model.

limitations: The ACS is currently limited to naturally conditioned spaces with operable windows, sedentary activity, and occupants able to adapt clothing.
The ACS does not apply when heating systems are in operation or mechanical cooling systems are present.
The use of mean monthly outdoor air temperature as input sacrifices resolution for practicality.
The ACS graph is truncated at 10°C and 33°C mean outdoor air temperature, leading to an unrealistic step change in allowable indoor temperatures outside this range.
Lack of sufficient hybrid ventilation (mixed-mode) buildings in the RP-884 database for separate analysis.
The GIS energy savings estimate is conservative and based on coarse data.
